final_proof:
Assume that \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\). The requested assertion is not presently a theorem, nor is it known to be false: it is exactly the Erdős–Moser conjecture.

Put \(m=k+1\). Since \(k\) is a positive integer, \(m\ge2\), and the equation becomes
\[
1^p+2^p+\cdots +(m-1)^p=m^p.
\]
Conversely, every positive-integer solution \((m,p)\) of this equation with \(m\ge2\) gives a solution of the original equation by taking \(k=m-1\). Thus this substitution is a bijection between the solutions of the stated problem and those of the classical Erdős–Moser equation. The conjecture that its only positive-integer solution is \((m,p)=(3,1)\) translates precisely into the claim that the only solution here is \((k,p)=(2,1)\). A proof of the requested claim would therefore settle that open conjecture, so no rigorous unconditional proof of the asserted uniqueness is currently available.

The unconditional correction that can be proved directly is: among solutions with \(p=1\), the unique solution is \(k=2\). Indeed, when \(p=1\),
\[
\frac{k(k+1)}2=k+1.
\]
Because \(k+1>0\), division by \(k+1\) gives \(k/2=1\), hence \(k=2\). Conversely,
\[
1^1+2^1=3=3^1,
\]
so \((k,p)=(2,1)\) is indeed a solution. Whether any solution with \(p>1\) exists is precisely the unresolved part of the Erdős–Moser conjecture.

If instead one uses the convention \(0\in\mathbb N\), then the statement as written also has the solution \((k,p)=(1,0)\), since \(1^0=2^0=1\). The customary formulation therefore requires a positive exponent.
